ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: On the left side of the circuit diagram there are three input terminals A, B, C. At the top is an “&” gate with a small circle at the output terminal, whose inputs come from A and B, indicating that the output is ¬(A·B). Below is another “&” gate with a small circle at the output terminal, whose inputs come from B and C, indicating that the output is ¬(B·C). These two outputs are connected to the gate on the right labeled “≥1”, which indicates that when at least one input is 1, the output is 1, namely OR logic. Reasoning: According to the method draft, translate the circuit as F = ¬(A·B) + ¬(B·C). When ABC = 111, A=1, B=1, C=1. Therefore ¬(A·B)=¬(1·1)=¬1=0, ¬(B·C)=¬(1·1)=¬1=0. The inputs of the OR/≥1 gate on the right are 0 and 0, so F=0. Final answer: 0.

planner_metadata.distinctiveness_rationale: Direct gate-by-gate evaluation from the drawn circuit; this is the natural single route for this simple combinational logic problem.
planner_metadata.image_role: Read the diagram as two left AND-shaped gates, each marked with a small inversion bubble at its output. The upper inverted-AND gate takes inputs A and B; the lower inverted-AND gate takes inputs B and C. Their two outputs feed a right-hand gate labeled “≥1”, i.e., an OR/at-least-one gate, whose output is F.
planner_metadata.text_role: Use the question statement to know the required input combination is ABC = 111 and that the requested value is the logical output F.
planner_metadata.knowledge_role: Use Boolean gate meanings: an AND gate with an output bubble is NAND, so its output is 0 only when all its inputs are 1; a “≥1” gate outputs 1 if at least one input is 1, otherwise 0.
